column2: The turning away from the impure with faith is better; he who has turned from faults of character and has faith is pure indeed.
What need has he of austerity, of conduct, of self? This person is made of faith; whoever has faith, he is that.
Thus dharma has been declared by the good who see the aims of dharma; we, wishing to know, have come to you to see dharma.
Give up rivalry, greatly wise one; then you will gain the highest; the trader, faithful and trusting, established in his own path, is the greater, Jajali."
Thus was spoken by Tuladhara a matter held in high esteem; and thus was he rightly rebuked, and eternal dharma was told.
Hearing the words of Tuladhara of renowned valour, that twice-born, Kaunteya, attained peace.
Then in no long time Tuladhara and he, the two greatly wise ones, going to heaven, took their pleasure happily, each gone to his own place won by the fruit of his own deeds.
For those who do what is called sacrifice, equal, faithful, restrained, of good mind, sacrifice is never unfit.
Faith is indeed the goddess of goodness, daughter of the sun, king, Savitri, the mother, and the one who trusts life.
Faith protects the aged in speech and in mind, Bharata, as taught by this comparison; what more do you wish to hear?"
Seeing the bull with cut sinews and the cows crying out greatly, in the seizure of cows at the sacrifice, that king, looking on,
said, "Good luck to the cows in the worlds!" Then a derivation was made: when violence had begun, this blessing was devised.
Violence has been declared by men who have no fixed limits, the deluded, unbelievers, doubting, obscure.
Manu, the righteous-souled, said that all action is non-violence toward oneself; out of desire and passion men kill animals outside the altar.
Therefore dharma, being subtle, must be known by one who knows with authority; non-violence alone is held greater than all dharmas.
Having fasted, sharpened, and given up the scriptural rules made in the Veda, the wretched, seeking fruit, call what is misconduct "conduct."
If men eat meat in vain, with sacrifices, trees and posts as their pretext, this dharma is not praised.
Meat, honey, liquor, fish, spirits and rice with sesame were introduced by rogues; this is not laid down in the Vedas.
[Yudhishthira said:] "The body and calamities dispute with one who is non-violent; how will the maintenance of the body of one who undertakes nothing succeed?"
[Bhishma said:] "Let him act in works so that the body does not waste away and does not fall under the power of death; being capable, he should practise dharma."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale of Chirakarin, which took place long ago in the family of Angiras.
Chirakarin, good luck to you; good luck to you, Chirakarin; for the wise Chirakarin does not err in his actions.
Chirakarin, greatly wise, was the son of Gautama; the thoughtful one comes to all tasks after a long time.
Thinking long on matters, long awake, long asleep, from reaching his tasks late, he is so called, Chirakarin.
He was called a dullard, taken as lazy, by people of light mind and short sight.
Once, in some case of misconduct, his father, angered, passing over his other sons, told him, "Kill this mother."
He said "so be it" after a long time, from his nature as Chirakarin; reflecting, from being a slow doer, he thought long.

How shall I do my father's command? How shall I not kill my mother? How can I escape this trap of dharma without becoming wicked?
mahabharata:12:258.11	Who ever becomes happy by killing a woman and his mother? And who gains standing by disregarding his father?
mahabharata:12:258.12	Not disregarding the father is fitting; supporting and protecting the mother is fitting; how may I not transgress these two, patience and propriety?
mahabharata:12:258.13	The father places himself in the wife, 'to be born,' for the upholding of the character, conduct and lineage of the family.
mahabharata:12:258.14	I am that self, made again by my father as a son; how should I not have knowledge, who have understood my own origin?
mahabharata:12:258.15	What the father said at the birth-rite and the initiation is the firm authority in the determination of the father's weight.
mahabharata:12:258.16	The teacher is the foremost, the highest dharma, beneficial through support and teaching; what the father says is dharma, well settled even in the Vedas.
mahabharata:12:258.17	The son is mere affection for the father; the father is all to the son; the body and the rest are to be given, and the father alone gives them.
mahabharata:12:258.18	Therefore the father's word is to be done, and not at all to be examined; even sins are purified for those who do the father's word.
mahabharata:12:258.19	In enjoyment, in fortune, in procreation, in all the world's evidence, in union with the husband, and at the parting of the hair,
mahabharata:12:258.20	the father is heaven, the father is dharma, the father is the highest austerity; when the father is pleased, all the deities are pleased.
mahabharata:12:258.21	The blessings a father speaks cling to that man; the father's delight is the atonement for all sins.
mahabharata:12:258.22	A flower is released from its bond, a fruit from its stalk; though troubled by love of the son, a father does not let go of affection.
mahabharata:12:258.23	This is the son's reflection on the father's weight; but I shall think of the mother as of lesser standing.
mahabharata:12:258.24	This aggregate in me of five elements in mortality: my mother is its cause, as the kindling-stick of fire; the mother is the kindling-stick of the body of men, the ease of everyone distressed.
mahabharata:12:258.25	He does not grieve, nor does the aged man drag him, who, though without a wife, calls mother" in his house.
He who is surrounded by sons and grandsons and resorts to his mother, at the end of a hundred years goes about like a two-year-old.
Whether capable or incapable, thin or not thin, the mother protects her son; no other is a supporter by rule.
He is old when he is afflicted; then the world is empty for him, then he is parted from his mother.
There is no shade like a mother, no goal like a mother, no protection like a mother, no water-stand like a mother.
By bearing in the womb she is the bearer, by giving birth the begetter; by nourishing the limbs, the mother; by bearing heroes, the mother of heroes.
By serving the child, she is the nurse; the mother is the body, next; what conscious man would kill her, whose head is not hollow?
The intent formed at the joining of the breaths of husband and wife, that the mother or father knows; the truth of the matter rests with the mother.
The mother knows the family and whose he is; the father has affection for his child through the mere nourishing by the mother.
Having himself taken her hand and come into shared dharma, if men then discard women, women do not deserve discarding.
A husband is bhartri by supporting women and pati by protecting women; when this quality is gone, he is neither bhartri nor pati.
So a woman does not offend; it is the man who offends; transgressing, committing a great fault, it is the man who offends.
For a woman the husband is the highest deity; he gave her to himself, like himself, as the highest; in all tasks women are not offenders.
He who speaks no direction of woman for satisfaction of union, as he recalls it clearly, there is certainly adharma; no doubt.
Even animals, though unwise, would know a woman and a mother as inviolable, standing in higher honour.
They hold the father as the assembly of the gods in one place; for mortals and gods, they approach the mother out of affection."
As he thus pondered at length, from being Chirakarin, a long time passed; then his father came.
Medhatithi, greatly wise Gautama, abiding in austerity, reflected that in that time he had transgressed the rule concerning his wife.
Burning with sorrow, shedding tears, he said, having come to remorse afterward through the grace of learning and steadiness:

Indra, lord of the three worlds, came to my hermitage, taking the vow of a guest and assuming the form of a brahmana.
mahabharata:12:258.45	He was comforted by her with words, honoured with welcome, and offered water for the feet and arghya properly by her.
mahabharata:12:258.46	'I am a chaste woman,' she said, 'I shall lead with policy'; in that mishap there is no transgression by the woman.
mahabharata:12:258.47	Thus neither the woman nor I nor the traveller, lord of the thirty gods, offends against dharma; it is heedlessness that offends.
mahabharata:12:258.48	They call it the calamity born of envy, and so for those of upward seed; by envy I was flung and sunk in an ocean of wrongdoing.
mahabharata:12:258.49	Having killed a virtuous woman, and chastised in calamity my wife who should be supported, who will carry me across?
mahabharata:12:258.50	If the noble-minded Chirakarin, commanded by me at the hour, should today be slow, he would save me from sin.
mahabharata:12:258.51	Chirakarin, good luck to you; if today you are Chirakarin, then you are truly Chirakarin.
mahabharata:12:258.52	Save me and your mother, and the austerity I have earned; save yourself from sins; be Chirakarin today.
mahabharata:12:258.53	Slowness is innate to you, from your long wisdom; let that slowness be fulfilled today; be Chirakarin today.
mahabharata:12:258.54	For long hoped for by your mother, for long carried in the womb: make your slowness fruitful, Chirakarin.
mahabharata:12:258.55	He delays from distress and sleeps long, restrained; see, Chirakarin, the long distress of us both.
So, king, the great sage Gautama, thus grieved, saw his son Chirakarin standing near.
Seeing his father, Chirakarin, in great sorrow, threw down his weapon and began to appease him with his head bowed.
Gautama, seeing his son fallen with head on the ground, and his wife formless, felt supreme joy.
For she had not been joined to him by that great soul, the wife in the lonely hermitage; and the son was collected.
One might kill, without blame, a son standing with weapon in hand; but having made him humble and modest, he should settle him in his own duties.
His thought, seeing his son bowed at his father's feet, was that the restlessness of taking up a weapon is covered by fear.
Then the father, praising him long, smelling his head long, embracing him long with his arms, long said, "Live long."
Thus Gautama, the greatly wise, joined with joy and delight, welcomed his son and spoke these words.
Chirakarin, good luck to you; be Chirakarin, long; while you were slow, I was greatly pained long.
The learned Gautama, best of sages, also spoke verses on the virtues of the slow-doers, the Chirakarins, as dreadful matters:

Slowly one should make a friend, and slowly give up what is done; for a friend made slowly deserves to be kept long.
mahabharata:12:258.67	In passion, pride and conceit, in treachery, in sin and in disagreeable deeds to be done, the slow-doer is praised.
mahabharata:12:258.68	With kinsmen, friends, servants and women, in unmanifest offences, the slow-doer is praised.
Thus Gautama was pleased with his son's deed, Bharata, Kauravya, and with that slowness.
Thus in all tasks, having reflected and made a decision slowly, one does not suffer long.
He holds his anger long, restrains action long; no deed that brings later remorse arises.
One should long attend the aged, long follow and honour, long practise dharmas, and long make inquiry.
Long following the learned, long serving the refined, long disciplining himself, he goes long unscorned.
Even the words of another that are joined with dharma one should long ask about and long speak; so he is long unrebuked."
Having lived many years there in that hermitage in great austerity, the brahmana went to heaven then with his son.
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Dyumatsena with the king Satyavan.
We have heard that Satyavan spoke what had not been said when men were being led to execution by his father's command:
Dharma goes to adharma and adharma goes to dharma; what is called killing as dharma cannot be so.
[Dyumatsena said:] "But if killing is not dharma, what could ever be dharma? If robbers were not slain, Satyavan, there would be confusion.
This is mine: that would not go on in the Kali age; and the course of the world would not be. If you know, tell us."
[Satyavan said:] "All three classes should be made subject to the brahmana; of those bound by the nooses of dharma, few will go astray.
Whoever of them goes astray, the twice-born should report, saying 'this one does not listen to me'; the king should then decide about him.
The scripture that is without difference of principle should be followed, not otherwise; killing, without examining actions, is not the policy-science as it is prescribed.
The root should not be struck; this is not eternal dharma; indeed atonement is ordained even without killing.
By harassment, bondage, disfigurement and the penalty of death they are to be afflicted, not before by the wealth of the harmful.
When they go to the priest for refuge, saying, 'Brahmana, we shall not do wrong again,'
then they should be released: so is the king's rule. A brahmana wearing the staff and deerskin, shaven, deserves clothing.
The more weighty, with repeated offence, deserve release again, but not as at the first."
[Dyumatsena said:] "Wherever the subjects can be restrained by agreement, so far dharma is said to be, so long as it is not transgressed.
When there is no killing, all would be defeated; earlier and still earlier people were easily ruled.
Gentle, mostly truthful, of little malice and little anger; formerly there was only the rod of 'Shame on you!' and then the rod of words.
There was also the rod of taking, and now the rod of killing is in use; and even by killing other people cannot be restrained.
The robber is not of men, nor of the gods, so it is heard, nor of gandharvas and ancestors; who here is anyone's?
He takes a lotus from the cremation ground and a deity from a pishacha; he who makes an agreement with the ignorant and dull-witted..."
[Satyavan said:] "If you cannot save the good by non-violence, then make an end by gaining something of the past and future."
[Dyumatsena said:] "Kings perform the highest austerity for the course of the world; they are ashamed before such men, and so they become.
Terrified, the virtuous do not kill evildoers by desire; kings rule the subjects mostly by virtue.
The world follows the better and better livelihood; men ever follow the conduct of the elder.
Men laugh at the one who, without restraining himself, wishes to restrain others, under the sway of senses in objects.
Whoever does something improper through the king's pride and delusion should be restrained by every means, and so he turns from sin.
One should first restrain oneself, for one who restrains evil; and punish with great punishments even near kinsmen.
Where a sinner is afflicted yet meets no great sorrow, there sins grow and dharma surely shrinks; so the learned brahmana of compassionate nature taught.
So I was instructed by earlier fathers and grandfathers, very much comforting me out of compassion.
In the first age, the Krita, the king followed this; by this dharma a quarter goes in the Treta, a half in the Dvapara, a quarter in the other age.
So in the Kali, by the kings' ill conduct, according to the particular time dharma would be a sixteenth part.
Then, Satyavan, by the first rule there would be confusion; stating life, power and time, one should enjoin austerity.
So that one not give up the great fruit of dharma for truth here, Manu the Self-born spoke, out of compassion for beings."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Of the dharma of the householder and the dharma of renunciation, both near at hand, which is the better, grandsire?"
[Bhishma said:] "Both dharmas are great, both very hard to practise, both of great fruit, dear, and both practised by the good.
Here I shall tell you the authority of both; hear, Partha, one-pointed, doubts in dharma and wealth cut.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Kapila and the cow; learn it, Yudhishthira.
Seeing the ancient, eternal, firm tradition, Nahusha formerly performed the offering of Tvashta's cow, so we have heard.
Her, thus engaged, Palila, undismayed in mind, abiding in goodness and devoted to rule, knowing, restrained in food, then saw.
Attaining the highest final understanding, free of fear, he said once, "I remember the loosened truth: the Vedas."
The sage Syumarashmi, entering that cow, said to the ascetic: "O Vedas! If the Vedas are authorities, by what are other dharmas held?
Ascetics, steadfast, with the eye of hearing and discernment, hold all the sages' utterances as known to the self.
For one so free of craving, free of fever, without hope and wholly without undertaking, what intent to speak is there about the Vedas?"
[Kapila said:] "I do not blame the Vedas nor ever wish to; we have heard that the works of those in different stages have one aim.
The renouncer goes and the forest-dweller goes; the householder and the celibate student, those two also go.
The four paths of the gods are held eternal; among them the greater and lesser differ; the strength and weakness is told in the fruits.
Having thus known all aims, one should undertake: so says the Vedic; elsewhere the final scripture says one should not undertake.
In not undertaking there would be no fault; in undertaking faultlessness is best; for a scripture so stated, the strength and weakness are hard to know.
If here you see anything direct, held higher than non-violence, apart from the scriptures of tradition, tell it."
[Syumarashmi said:] "'One desiring heaven should sacrifice': so scripture is constantly heard; having first imagined the fruit, the sacrifice is then extended.
Goat, horse, ram, cow, and flocks of birds, village and forest herbs: food for breath, so scripture says.
Likewise food is offered day by day, evening and morning; animals and grain are a limb of sacrifice, so scripture says.
These together with sacrifice Prajapati devised; by it the lord Prajapati sacrificed to the gods by sacrifice.
They all say that these moving beings, seven and seven, are equal to each other; the universe offered in sacrifices is called the highest.
And this was approved by earlier and still earlier; what learned man would not examine his own power?
Animals, men, trees with herbs wish for heaven alone, and there is no heaven without sacrifice.
Herbs, animals, trees, creepers, ghee, milk, curds, oblation, earth, the quarters, faith and time: these twelve.
The Rik, Yajus and Saman verses, and the sacrificer as sixteenth; fire, the householder, is known as seventeenth. These are the limbs of sacrifice; sacrifice is the root, so scripture says.
With ghee, milk, curds, dung, curd-cheese, skin, hair, horn and foot the cow becomes the sacrifice; so each is for whatever is ordained for it.
They carry the sacrifice together, with priests and fees; all these together bring the sacrifice to completion.
These are created for sacrifice, as scripture is heard; so the earlier and still earlier men acted.
He who sacrifices without desire for fruit, thinking 'sacrifice must be done,' neither harms nor betrays anyone.
These limbs of sacrifice, as stated, without doubt, joined by rule, carry each other across.
I see the tradition of the sages in which the Vedas are established; the learned see it by following the brahmana.
Sacrifice has the brahmana as its source and is offered to the brahmana; the whole world follows sacrifice and sacrifice follows the world.
Om is the womb of Brahman; salutation, svaha, svadha, vashat: for him who uses these, even if done as far as he is able,
they say he has no fear of the next world in the three worlds: so the Vedas say here, and the perfected and great sages.
The Rik, Yajus, Saman and stobha verses enjoined by rule: the twice-born in whom all these are only outward.
In the setting up of the fires, in the soma pressing, twice-born, and in the other great sacrifices, the blessed Veda knows it of itself.
Therefore, brahmana, one should sacrifice and cause to sacrifice without doubting; for the sacrificer, by the rule of heaven, there is great fruit of heaven after death.
This world is not for the non-sacrificers, nor the next: so it is settled; the knowers of Vedic disputation also hold both as authority."
[Kapila said:] "This body acts so, and in the Veda it makes a form; the brahmana whose body has been purified by rites becomes a vessel.
I tell you of him who pursues the endless by action: without tradition, without legend, direct, with the world as witness.

Those who spread out sacrifices as "dharma" alone, without hope, renouncing what has arisen, ungreedy, as if earned by compassion and freedom from envy: this is the road of wealth, in giving at holy places.
Not depending on action as a womb, sinful deeds at times, perfected by mental intention, of purified settled knowledge,
not angry, not envious, without ego or malice, devoted to knowledge, thrice-white, intent on the good of all beings:
householders were mostly such, not departing from their own duties, and kings joined in this way, and brahmanas by rule.
Equal, endowed with honesty, content, resolved in knowledge, with dharma visible, pure, faithful toward higher and lower,
with selves formed before, who had duly practised their vows, they practised dharma even in hardship and gathered in difficult places.
Since such were the brahmanas of old, carriers of sacrifice, aged in the three Vedas, pure, well-conducted and renowned, wise, sacrificing day by day, without hope or bonds,
for them sacrifices, Vedas and deeds were as the tradition, as the seasons, as intentions according to their vows.
For those who had shed desire and anger, by nature trained in self, honest, constant in calm, standing in their own duties, all was endless: so we have the eternal scripture.
For those of undismayed goodness, doers of hard conduct, covered by their own deeds, the dreadfulness of austerity came about.
That good conduct, wonderful, ancient, eternal and firm, was indicated in the dharmas for those unable to practise it at all.
Dharma without calamity, conduct, heedfulness and non-defeat, among all classes: among them there was no transgression.
Those bulls among men took refuge in one four-footed dharma; the good, having duly reached it, go to the highest goal.
Some, leaving their homes, resorted to the forest; others, resorting to the home alone; and others, celibate students.
Brahmanas know this fourfold dharma of stages; the endless seat of Brahman is the settled meaning of the word brahmana.
Therefore such brahmanas of old, who practised dharma, are seen in heaven as twice-born become lights.
Like stars in their places, many hosts of stars, they have reached the endless through contentment: so the Vedic.
If such come back to the world, in a womb again, they are never stained by sinful deeds, not by action as a womb.
One so joined may be a brahmana; another may be a brahmana in name; action alone, good or bad, they say, belongs to man.
So, for those whose astringency is ripened, by endless learning, all was endless: so we have the eternal scripture.
For them, craving gone, cleansed, of good self, the fourth, the dharma of the Upanishads, is held common.
It is ever practised by the perfected brahmanas of controlled self, rooted in contentment, of the nature of renunciation, called based on knowledge.
The ascetic's eternal dharma, whose goal is liberation, is practised as common or sole according to strength.
As one goes and goes, the weak sinks in it; seeking the seat of Brahman, the pure one is freed from the world."
[Syumarashmi said:] "Of those who enjoy, those who give, who sacrifice, who study, those who by means gained by dharma, or those who rely on renunciation,
which of these, after death, is the best conqueror of heaven? Tell me that, brahmana, as I ask truly."
[Kapila said:] "All good possessions and the good fortunes that arise from virtue are not the happiness reached by renunciation; you too see this."
[Syumarashmi said:] "You are devoted to knowledge, we householders resolved on action; of all stages the end is said to be one."
In oneness and in separateness no other difference is told; let the blessed one tell me that rightly and properly."
[Kapila said:] "Actions are the ripening of the body, but knowledge is the highest goal; when astringency is ripened, vomiting does not remain in the knowledge of taste.
Non-cruelty, forbearance, peace, non-violence, truth, honesty, non-malice, no pride, modesty, patience and self-control:
these are the paths of Brahman; by them one reaches the supreme; the learned man should understand by mind the settled rule of action.
The goal which brahmanas, calm on every side, pure, resolved in knowledge, content, reach: they call it the highest goal.
Having known the Vedas and what is to be known, as it stands, thus they call a Veda-knower; another is a mere seed-keeper.
The Veda-knowers know all; all is established in the Veda; for in the Veda is the end of everything, of whatever is and is not."
What fault could be mine or yours, best of the twice-born, by which Agni was lost, as if done among wicked men?
The king Marutta was pure and virtuous; even Shakra, though striving, did not surpass him.
I have lived long, son, and long been served by you; you ought to give leave to me, aged, king.
Let Arjuna quickly come here, having heard that the Yadavas are slain by a Brahmana's curse. Thus addressed, Daruka, his mind lost, went in the chariot to the Kurus.
You have reached the highest success as no other man ever has; your brothers have not reached that place, delight of the Kurus.
Dear, enjoy the fruit of your holy deeds, won by austerity yourself, and of your gifts, mighty-armed Pandava.
